canonical_statement: The study formalizes streaming dialogue summarization as generating a self-contained summary of a current dialogue window using selectively constructed memory from an unbounded prior history under a fixed budget.
The authors argue that the central challenge is whether memory recovers evidence presupposed by the current window, rather than the total amount of dialogue history accessed.

ReMEMBER is a two-stage missing-evidence memory framework that first retrieves history conditioned on unresolved window dependencies and then refines retrieved chunks into evidence-dense memory under a fixed token budget.

At step t, the model observes a recent-utterance window W_t, treats all preceding utterances as history H_t, constructs a bounded memory M_t, and generates a self-contained summary S_t of W_t using the historical evidence needed to resolve contextual gaps.
The benchmark is built from 35 long dialogues spanning chit-chat and workplace domains: LoCoMo and RealTalk21 contribute 20 chit-chat dialogues, and EverMemBench contributes 15 workplace dialogues.

population.label: 35 source dialogues from LoCoMo, RealTalk21, and EverMemBench

canonical_statement: Each dialogue is segmented into 1,024-token current windows, with all preceding utterances serving as the accumulated history for that benchmark candidate.
Benchmark candidates are excluded when the accumulated history is shorter than 7K tokens or when all salient utterances in the current window are self-contained.

population.label: Candidate 1,024-token dialogue windows
inclusion_criteria: Accumulated history of at least 7K tokens
At least one history-dependent salient utterance

canonical_statement: The construction pipeline produced 1,079 eligible candidates with history lengths from 7K to 160K tokens, from which 900 benchmark instances were sampled with domain stratification.

Contextual gaps are grouped into three history-resolvable types: referential gaps for missing antecedents, attribute gaps for missing states or properties, and relational gaps for missing causal, logical, temporal, or discourse relations.

Salient utterances and contextual gaps are produced through a five-stage LLM-assisted annotation pipeline; each stage uses three independent model families and retains outputs only by majority agreement.
Memory recall is the proportion of annotated contextual gaps for which the constructed memory explicitly contains the corresponding resolving information.

outcome.definition: Fraction of annotated gaps whose resolving information is present in memory

canonical_statement: Window completeness is the fraction of salient current-window utterances whose primary content is covered by the generated summary.

outcome.definition: Fraction of salient utterances covered by the summary

canonical_statement: Gap-resolution completeness measures the fraction of memory-resolved contextual gaps whose minimal resolving fact is expressed in the generated summary.

outcome.definition: Fraction of memory-resolved gaps reflected in the summary

canonical_statement: Conciseness is the proportion of summary sentences that either cover at least one salient current-window utterance or explicitly express at least one gap-resolving fact.

outcome.definition: Proportion of summary sentences serving salient-window coverage or gap-resolution functions

canonical_statement: Faithfulness is evaluated at the atomic-fact level by decomposing summary sentences into self-contained verifiable claims and measuring the fraction judged factually grounded.

outcome.definition: Fraction of decomposed atomic facts judged grounded

canonical_statement: At inference time, ReMEMBER identifies current-window utterances that are both summary-worthy and dependent on prior dialogue, then converts each unresolved dependency into an evidence-seeking query without hypothesizing the missing answer.
Qwen3.5-4B is the default compact model used for gap detection, operating only on the current window without benchmark annotations, resolving evidence, or gap-type labels.
The accumulated history is segmented into 128-token candidate chunks with 32-token overlap for evidence retrieval.
Each gap query is sent to BM25 sparse retrieval and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B dense retrieval, and the two ranked lists are fused using reciprocal rank fusion.
Each sparse and dense retriever returns the top 30 chunks per gap before fusion and refinement.

ReMEMBER refines each retrieved chunk by embedding its constituent utterances against the gap query, ranking turns by cosine similarity, and retaining complete high-scoring speaker turns as evidence units.
Turn-level evidence is accumulated round-robin across detected gaps until the fixed memory budget is reached so that no single gap monopolizes memory capacity.
For summary generation, all memory strategies use a generator that receives only the constructed memory and the current window; the generator is otherwise held fixed across memory strategies.
The experiments fix both the current-window size and memory capacity at 1,024 tokens across memory construction methods.
The comparison includes diagnostic references (Ideal Memory, No Memory, Full Memory) and recency-, summarization-, and retrieval-based bounded-memory baselines under the same capacity constraint.
All reported memory and summary metrics are scored by Qwen3.6-27B at temperature 0.0 using rubric-guided prompts.
Summary evaluation results are averaged across Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-9B, and Gemma-4-E2B-it summarizers run at temperature 0.7.
All model runs use a single NVIDIA H200 GPU, and all results are reported from a single experimental run.
ReMEMBER achieved overall memory recall of 0.6984 versus 0.5412 for Hybrid, the strongest memory-construction baseline in Table 1.

In the annotation pipeline, candidate history chunks are labeled relevant only when they contain prior content necessary or directly useful for understanding or summarizing the current window; topical similarity alone is explicitly insufficient.

Evidence annotation audits each sentence independently and accepts a resolving sentence only when it explicitly supplies the exact missing referent, attribute, prior decision, or commitment required by the target gap; topical overlap and discourse proximity alone do not qualify.

Final annotation validation jointly requires sufficient, non-inferential, independence-supporting, and non-redundant evidence, with majority agreement across Qwen3.6-27B, Gemma-4-31B-it, and GLM-4.7-Flash.
In the chit-chat domain, ReMEMBER achieved memory recall of 0.6918, compared with 0.5519 for the strongest domain-specific baseline (Hierarchical Summary).
In the workplace domain, ReMEMBER achieved memory recall of 0.7018, compared with 0.5719 for the strongest domain-specific baseline (Hybrid).

The authors state that experiments use existing research datasets and open-weight language models, that model checkpoints are publicly accessible through Hugging Face, and that benchmark statistics and implementation details are provided in the appendices.
The authors report using Codex for coding assistance and Claude for grammar checking during preparation of the paper.

The authors conclude that ReMEMBER improves memory recall and gap-resolution completeness under the same memory budget across histories up to 160K tokens by constructing memory around detected contextual gaps rather than surface similarity.

The authors conclude that even when reference gap-resolving evidence is supplied, summary generation remains an independent bottleneck because recovered evidence is not always reflected in the output summary.
